Oh, shit. I guess it was below the fold when I asked. My apologies. As for employment, look for small businesses in your area. I guarantee that most of their websites look like shit, are slow, poorly optimized for web crawlers and haven't been updated in months. These same businesses know that their web presence is hugely important to survival for small companies in this era, but they just don't know how to get it right without paying a ton of money. Approach a few, offer to do a little bit of work for cheap maintaining it. Not the full time stuff that many marketing firms offer (since most small businesses can't afford such services, which has kept their websites stifled), but just a little bit here and there, make sure that the top post on the site is from that month, that any press coverage they get is updated, and that a product catalog is available and up to date (if relevant). Its not glamorous (seriously, I hate playing the webmaster, that was the first part of the tech business that I insisted the company I work for outsource, and i'm still pretty unsatisfied with how much I have to fuck with it), but its better than being underemployed. The modest requirements I listed means that, at the very most, its a 4 hour a week position, meaning you can pick up 5 or 6 of them, while still leaving LOTS of time to search for a job more to your liking. Who knows, one of them might also take a liking to you and offer a larger position managing all their tech, which can range from 10 hours a week to full time and then some depending on industry and exact company size. Protip, though, as someone who works high in the pecking order of such a small business, DO NOT EMAIL THEM. Period. End of discussion. It won't get seen, especially since the companies you would be targeting are the ones that likely just bought a domain+ hosting combo off godaddy/ wix.etc (which means they get a TON of spam email related to their website). Call, or show up in person, and be prepared for a bit of a wait. If the business is under 100 people, and isn't an exclusively whitecollar company (say foodservice or manufacturing vs tech services or a creative firm, though if either of the latter need a webmaster, we have bigger problems to deal with), its entirely possible that the owner is the only person involved in the hiring and staffing decisions, at least officially, and these people are unimaginably busy (my boss has been putting in 60-80 hour weeks for the past 7 years, depending on the season, with only 2 vacations of over a week in the same period).

If you enjoy the repair side of technology, go grab a compTIA A+ certification. That's enough to get your foot in the door at a computer repair shop or in the IT support department of most businesses that aren't themselves in the tech industry, assuming your resume doesn't have any huge red flags, and you aren't too ambitious with the positions you apply for. A quick trip to a used bookstore should get you some certification study guides for about 20 bucks. Alternatively, if you are lacking work experience in general, a compTIA IT for Sales cert is only 100, and while these things are worth about as much as toilet paper (take it from someone who has one), it looks VERY impressive to people who don't know what they're talking about, you should be able to land a job on the floor at best buy or another electronics retailer, and be on the short list next time they need to promote someone. It might only be tangentially related to IT, and therefore not great for a resume but if you can swallow your pride long enough to get into a management position, even if its trivial, like overseeing the 3 salespeople who work in the washer/dryer aisles, it starts looking considerably better than unemployed or fast food on a resume. Plus, if there's one thing IT workers lack, its soft skills. A sales job will tell anyone looking at your resume that you can deal with people, a desired quality in the desktop support world, a management position with a good reference will scream that.

If you need good Virtualization I highly recommened VMWare Player. They offer a free version for non-commercial use which is pretty cool. VirtualBox is very good but it's lacking in the 3d Support. Alot of games will not draw correctly even with 3d support enabled.
